title: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.
lead: Red Owl repeatedly assured Joseph Hoffman that he could obtain a grocery franchise and directed sales and expenditures along the way. Although the negotiations never produced a complete franchise agreement, Wisconsin allowed recovery for proved losses caused by reliance on those assurances.

actors.name: Joseph and Mrs. Hoffman
actors.role: Bakery owners pursuing a Red Owl grocery franchise

proceedings: Jury found reliance and assessed damages; trial court ordered a new trial on grocery-sale damages alone; Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed on appeal and cross-appeal.
limits: The extended early chronology comes from the assigned casebook introduction; the full brief separately identifies the opinion’s findings and analysis. No separate opinion or numerical vote alignment is supplied. This is a transformation of that source, not a new opinion audit.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An $18,000 franchise plan
paragraphs: Joseph Hoffman and his wife operated a bakery in Wautoma, Wisconsin. Beginning in 1959, Hoffman discussed a Red Owl grocery franchise with the company’s representative, Lukowitz. Hoffman said he had only $18,000 to invest, and Lukowitz repeatedly assured him that amount would suffice.

In February 1961, Hoffman bought a small grocery store to learn the business. The store began profitably, and summer tourists promised more business. Nevertheless, in June, Lukowitz advised Hoffman to sell it and assured him Red Owl would establish him in a larger store. Hoffman followed that advice.

sections.title: The Hoffmans sell and relocate as the financing demands rise
paragraphs: On Red Owl’s advice, Hoffman paid $1,000 toward a Chilton lot selected for the venture. Lukowitz said preparations were ready and told him to assemble the money. Red Owl then urged the sale of the bakery building as the last necessary step. The Hoffmans sold it in November at a $2,000 loss.

Hoffman rented a Chilton home for one month at $125. The family instead moved to Neenah after Red Owl suggested further experience at a Fox River Valley store. That job never materialized. Hoffman worked nights in an Appleton bakery while remaining available for Red Owl work; moving cost $140.

Meanwhile, Red Owl raised the required investment from $18,000 to $24,100, then said another $2,000 would permit the transaction. The parties considered money from Hoffman’s father-in-law, including a partnership arrangement, but Red Owl wanted an outright gift or subordinated funds. A final proposed statement called for $34,000, including a $13,000 gift from the father-in-law. Hoffman refused. Negotiations collapsed with the building’s size, cost, design, and layout unresolved, along with important lease terms governing rent, maintenance, renewal, and purchase.

sections.title: A jury finds induced reliance
paragraphs: The Hoffmans sued Red Owl and Lukowitz. A special verdict found the necessary representations, reliance with ordinary care, and Hoffman’s fulfillment of the conditions demanded during negotiations. The jury awarded $16,735 for the grocery sale, $2,000 for the bakery loss, $1,000 for the lot payment, $140 for moving, and $125 for rent.

The trial court upheld the latter four amounts but ordered a new trial limited to grocery-sale damages. Red Owl appealed liability and all damage items. The Hoffmans cross-appealed the partial new-trial order. Red Owl’s central argument was that promises too indefinite to create a franchise contract were also insufficient for promissory estoppel.

sections.title: Wisconsin recognizes a remedy for the promises actually made
paragraphs: Chief Justice Currie’s opinion adopted Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90 as an affirmative basis for relief. A promise must foreseeably induce definite and substantial action or forbearance, actually cause that reliance, and require enforcement to prevent injustice. The first two questions ordinarily belong to the jury; the last requires judicial judgment about policy and remedy.

The evidence supported the jury’s findings concerning Red Owl’s assurances, Hoffman’s reasonable reliance, and his compliance with the imposed conditions. The court rejected a requirement that the promises contain every term of an offer capable of acceptance. Although promissory estoppel sometimes supplied consideration for an otherwise complete gratuitous promise, its role was broader. Here, particular assurances induced particular sales and expenditures before a final franchise bargain existed.

Fraud did not supply an adequate alternative. A promise of future performance is fraudulent only when made with a present intention not to perform, and the record did not establish such bad faith by Lukowitz. Proved detrimental reliance could warrant relief even without that mental state. The court’s approach still required promises, foreseeable and actual reliance, and injustice; unsuccessful negotiations alone did not suffice.

sections.title: Four losses survive appellate review
paragraphs: The $2,000 bakery loss was supported. Although Mrs. Hoffman had not personally negotiated, Red Owl had foreseen and requested sale of her jointly owned interest. Her share could therefore be recovered.

The $1,000 lot payment was part of the purchase price after exercise of an option, creating equity in the land. Red Owl argued that the equity was already lost because another $5,000 was overdue or that Hoffman should have paid the balance to preserve property possibly worth $6,000. No foreclosure of his equity was shown, and avoiding the loss did not reasonably require another $5,000 commitment after the franchise plan failed.

The $125 rent followed assurances that the bakery sale would finish preparations. The $140 move resulted from that induced sale and the relocation plan. Both were proper reliance losses, even though the family ultimately moved to Neenah rather than Chilton.

sections.title: The largest award requires a new trial
paragraphs: The grocery-sale award lacked adequate proof of the difference between fair market value, including supported goodwill, and the sale proceeds. Hoffman bought $9,000 of inventory, added $1,500, and sold it for $10,000. Equipment bought for $7,000 sold for $7,955.96 according to his tax return. The buyer’s evidence of $44,000 in sales and $6,000 gross profit over eleven weeks did not establish a $16,735 loss.

The store had been a temporary learning venture, with a larger location already contemplated. Justice did not require compensation for every profit Hoffman might have earned by keeping it. Anticipated summer profits were not recoverable as though a franchise contract had been breached, although properly founded expert evidence could use profits to value goodwill.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the order, preserving the four smaller awards and requiring a new trial on the grocery’s proved fair-market-value shortfall. Because the Hoffmans had cross-appealed, they could tax only two-thirds of their costs. Rehearing was denied with costs on April 27, 1965.
